title: The Future of Electric Cars
description: Four recordings about electric cars: an interview, a conversation between friends, a lecture on batteries and a podcast about charging.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Mai, interviewing Dr Hall, an expert on transport.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Welcome to Morning Science. Today I'm talking to Dr Hall, who studies transport. Dr Hall, will petrol cars really disappear?

script.speaker: Dr Hall
script.text: Well, not overnight, Mai. Many countries plan to stop selling new petrol cars in about ten years, but millions of old cars will still be on the roads long after that.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So the change will be gradual. What is slowing it down?

script.speaker: Dr Hall
script.text: Mostly price. An electric car still costs more to buy, although it's cheaper to run. People look at the sticker price and get nervous, which is a pity, because over five years many drivers actually save money.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I've heard that some people worry about range, too.

script.speaker: Dr Hall
script.text: Yes, and honestly, I think that worry is bigger than the real problem. The average driver travels about thirty miles a day, and most modern electric cars can manage over two hundred miles on one charge. The fear is mostly psychological.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: What about the environment? Aren't the batteries terrible for the planet?

script.speaker: Dr Hall
script.text: That's a fair question. Making a battery does create a lot of pollution. But after a year or two of driving, an electric car has usually made up for that, especially if the electricity comes from wind or sun.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So you're optimistic.

script.speaker: Dr Hall
script.text: Cautiously, yes. I'd say the technology is ready. It's the habits and the budgets that need to catch up.

parts.title: Part 2 · Choosing a car
parts.intro: You will hear two friends, Nam and Linh, discussing Nam's plan to buy a car.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Linh, I've finally decided. I'm going to buy an electric car next month.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Really? I thought you wanted a second-hand petrol one. What changed your mind?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: My fuel bill, mainly. I spend nearly two hundred pounds a month driving to work. Charging at home would cost about a third of that.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Hmm. But what about charging? We live in a flat, Nam. You don't have a driveway.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's the one thing that worries me. There's a public charger at the end of our street, though, and my office has four more in the car park.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Four chargers for how many staff? Forty? You might wait ages.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Well, no, because most of my colleagues drive petrol cars. I'd say I'd only have to queue once a week at the most.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I'm still not convinced. My cousin bought one last year and he says the battery lost power in the cold.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Yes, that happens a little in winter, but it's not dramatic. He probably just expected too much.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Maybe. Anyway, I'd test drive a few before deciding. Promise me you'll do that.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I promise. Actually, I've already booked one for Saturday morning. Do you want to come?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Go on, then. But I'm driving first.

parts.title: Part 3 · A lecture on batteries
parts.intro: You will hear part of a university lecture given by Professor Bennett.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at the part of an electric car that matters most: the battery.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: Most batteries today use lithium, a light metal that stores a lot of energy for its weight. The problem is that lithium has to be mined, and mining uses a great deal of water.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: Researchers are therefore working on alternatives. One promising idea is a battery made with sodium, which is found in ordinary salt. Sodium batteries are cheaper, although at the moment they store less energy.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: Another development is the solid-state battery. Instead of liquid inside, it has a solid material, which makes it safer and allows faster charging. Some laboratories claim they can reach eighty per cent in ten minutes.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: I'd be careful with those claims, though. Laboratory results often look wonderful, but it can take ten years to turn an idea into a product that millions of people can buy.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: Recycling is the third area. At present only about half of old batteries are recycled, but new factories should raise that figure significantly by the end of this decade.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: So what should we conclude? In my view, no single breakthrough will solve everything. Progress will come from many small improvements, and that, frankly, is how most technology has always developed.

script.speaker: Professor Bennett
script.text: For next week, please read the article on the reading list and think about which of these three areas you consider most important.

parts.title: Part 4 · A podcast about charging
parts.intro: You will hear Minh, the presenter of a podcast, talking to Hannah, who runs a charging company.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Welcome back to Green Roads. This week, I'm joined by Hannah, who runs a charging company. Hannah, what's the biggest myth about charging?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: That it takes hours. Yes, at home overnight it does, but you're asleep anyway. On a motorway, a fast charger can add a lot of range in about twenty minutes, which is roughly the time you'd stop for coffee.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: And yet I still see queues at some stations.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: True, and that's frustrating. The problem isn't the number of chargers overall, it's where they are. We have lots in cities, but far fewer in villages and on small roads.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: So who is responsible for fixing that?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Everyone, really. Companies like mine, local councils, even supermarkets. Actually, supermarkets are doing the most useful thing, because people can charge while they shop.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: What about the price? I've heard public charging can be dearer than petrol.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Sometimes, yes, and I won't pretend otherwise. Home charging is the cheap option. Public charging is for convenience, so I'd advise people to use it only when they need to.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Last question. If you could give one piece of advice to a new owner, what would it be?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Plan the first long trip carefully. Once you've done it once and seen it works, the worry disappears.
